checks.prompt: An agent must, for each of five products, look up a unit price, look up stock, multiply them, and report the largest. Contrast how a structured-tool-call agent and this library's default agent express that. What is the concrete difference and where does it come from?
checks.explanation: The bet behind this library is that the natural action for a model that is already good at writing Python is Python. A structured call expresses one invocation with one set of arguments — chaining two tools takes two round trips, and looping or holding an intermediate value is not expressible at all, so composition has to be reassembled by the framework across turns. A code blob can call several tools, bind variables, loop and branch in a single action, which is why the same task takes fewer steps and fewer tokens.
options: The structured-call agent needs a separate round trip per tool invocation and has no way to loop or hold intermediate values, so the work becomes ten calls plus a final comparison assembled through more structured messages. This library's default agent writes ONE snippet of Python that loops over the products, calls both tools inside the loop, keeps the totals in a variable and returns the maximum — fewer steps and fewer tokens, because the action representation itself can express iteration and composition
Both express it identically; the difference is only the serialisation format of the action, so the number of model calls is the same and the choice is a matter of taste
The structured-call agent handles it in one call by passing a list of items, whereas the code-writing agent must still call each tool separately because tools are executed outside the interpreter
The code-writing agent is slower here because every statement is executed as its own step and fed back as an observation before the next statement runs

checks.prompt: Describe this library's default agent as a programmer at an interactive Python session, naming who plays which role. Walk through one iteration of the loop, saying exactly what the observation is. Explain what ends the loop and what happens if that never occurs. Then explain the relationship between this and the classic reason-act-observe loop, and what the library's second agent type changes.
checks.expected: A correct answer must assign the roles: the model is the programmer and the library provides the interactive session, in which the registered tools are already ordinary functions in scope. One iteration must be walked through: the model reads the task and the history so far and writes a snippet of code as its action; the library executes that snippet in its interpreter; and the observation fed back is what the code printed, together with any error it raised. That loop repeats. What ends it must be named precisely: a special built-in function the code calls with the answer, which terminates the run and returns that value. If the model never calls it, the run continues to a hard cap on iterations and then fails — which is why that cap matters and why truncated-looking results usually mean the model is not terminating. The relationship to the classic loop must be stated: this IS reason, act, observe, with the action being executable code rather than a parsed tool-name-and-argument string; everything else about the loop is the same. The second agent type must be described as emitting a conventional structured tool call instead of code, chosen when the backend's native tool-calling is stronger or when a capability must not be expressible as free-form code — same library, same loop, different action representation. Noting that state persists across steps, so a variable bound in one action is available in the next, is a plus.

checks.prompt: A team is configuring the interpreter that runs the model's code. Their agent's task needs data analysis, so a developer proposes allowing every module the code might want, including one for running shell commands, on the grounds that 'we can always tighten it later'. Another says the interpreter is a sandbox, so it does not matter. Assess both positions.
checks.explanation: Two separate points, both important. The import allow-list is a footgun in both directions: too narrow and the agent's code keeps failing on modules it legitimately needs, too wide and you have given a model your shell — permitting a command-running module makes the rest of the restriction pointless. And the local interpreter is explicitly a guardrail rather than a jail: it stops unauthorised imports and obvious hazards, but it is not hardened, so untrusted input or production deployment needs genuine isolation — a container or a hosted sandbox executor.
options: The allow-list should carry the minimum the task needs: too narrow and the agent's code keeps erroring, too wide and you have handed the model a shell — a module for running commands defeats the entire restriction. And the second position is wrong in an important way: the local interpreter is a guardrail, not a jail. It blocks unauthorised imports and obviously dangerous operations, but it is not a hardened sandbox, so untrusted tasks or production use call for real isolation such as a container or a hosted sandbox executor
The wide allow-list is fine because the interpreter intercepts dangerous calls regardless of which modules are imported, and the second developer is right that isolation is already complete
The allow-list is advisory only and affects error messages rather than execution, so neither position matters; what protects you is the step cap
Both are wrong because the interpreter executes nothing locally — code always runs in a remote hosted sandbox, so the allow-list only controls which packages get installed there

checks.prompt: Implement the code-action loop. Define `FinalAnswer(Exception)` carrying a `value`, and `MaxStepsError(Exception)`. Write `make_namespace(tools, authorized_imports)` returning the globals the model's code runs in: a `__builtins__` mapping exposing at least `print`, `len`, `sum`, `range`, `round`, `sorted`, `min`, `max` and `abs` from the real builtins, plus an `__import__` replacement that raises `ImportError("import of 'x' is not allowed")` unless the FIRST dotted component of the module name is in `authorized_imports` and otherwise delegates to the real one; a `final_answer(value)` function that raises `FinalAnswer(value)`; and every entry of the `tools` dict (name to callable) bound as a plain global. Write `run_code_agent(task, model, tools, authorized_imports=(), max_steps=6)`: build the namespace ONCE so state persists between steps, then up to `max_steps` times call `model(task, )` and take the text between the first `` and `` (which may span lines). With no such block, append `{"code": None, "observation": "No block found in your reply"}` and continue. Otherwise execute the code in that namespace with standard output captured: if `FinalAnswer` is raised, return `{"answer": , "steps": <1-based step>, "history": }`; if any other exception is raised, the observation is `": "`; otherwise it is the captured output, stripped. Append `{"code", "observation"}` to the history and continue. Raise `MaxStepsError` if the cap is reached with no final answer. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Two properties here are the whole argument for code as the action. The first snippet calls two tools, multiplies their results and returns — one action for work that a one-invocation-per-turn action representation would spread over several turns. And the namespace is built once, so a variable bound in one step is still there in the next: the session persists, which is what makes multi-step computation natural. The import guard is the other half. Notice it fires on the ROOT of the module name, so reaching for a submodule of a forbidden package is refused too, and notice that the refusal is an observation rather than a crash — the model reads it and reaches for something it is allowed. That is the same mechanism handling every other failure: an undefined name, a key that is not there, or a reply with no code block at all each come back as text to correct from. And nothing ends the run except the terminating call, which is why the cap exists and why an agent that never calls it fails rather than quietly returning something.
checks.test: def get_price(item: str) -> float: """Return the unit price of a grocery item.""" return {"apple": 0.50, "banana": 0.30}.get(item.lower(), 1.00) def stock(item: str) -> int: """How many are in stock.""" return {"apple": 12, "banana": 3}[item] TOOLS = {"get_price": get_price, "stock": stock} def scripted(*blobs): state = {"i": -1} def model(task, history): state["i"] += 1 return blobs[state["i"]] return model # One blob calls two tools, does arithmetic and returns -- work that would be # several separate round trips if the action had to be a single structured call. run = run_code_agent("total value of the apples", scripted( "Thought: multiply price by stock.\n" "\nfinal_answer(get_price('apple') * stock('apple'))\n"), TOOLS) assert run["answer"] == 6.0, run assert run["steps"] == 1, run # Variables survive between steps, because the interpreter session persists: the # second blob uses a name the first one bound. run = run_code_agent("cost of 6 apples", scripted( "\nunit = get_price('apple')\ntotal = unit * 6\nprint('unit', unit)\n", "\nfinal_answer(total)\n"), TOOLS) assert run["answer"] == 3.0, run assert run["steps"] == 2, run # Whatever the code printed is the observation handed back to the model. assert run["history"][0]["observation"] == "unit 0.5", run["history"] # Imports are refused unless they were explicitly allowed -- and the refusal is an # observation the model can react to, not a crash. run = run_code_agent("area of a circle", scripted( "\nimport os\nprint(os.listdir('.'))\n", "\nimport math\nfinal_answer(round(math.pi, 3))\n"), TOOLS, authorized_imports=["math"]) assert "not allowed" in run["history"][0]["observation"], run["history"][0] assert run["history"][0]["observation"].startswith("ImportError"), run["history"][0] assert run["answer"] == 3.142, run # With nothing allowed, even a harmless standard module is refused. run = run_code_agent("x", scripted("\nimport math\nfinal_answer(1)\n", "\nfinal_answer(0)\n"), TOOLS) assert run["answer"] == 0 and "ImportError" in run["history"][0]["observation"], run # A submodule is judged by its root package. run = run_code_agent("x", scripted( "\nimport os.path\n", "\nfinal_answer('done')\n"), TOOLS) assert "'os'" in run["history"][0]["observation"], run["history"][0] # Any other failure comes back as an observation too, so a capable model corrects # itself on the next step instead of the run dying. run = run_code_agent("x", scripted( "\nfinal_answer(get_prices('apple'))\n", "\nfinal_answer(get_price('apple'))\n"), TOOLS) assert run["history"][0]["observation"].startswith("NameError"), run["history"][0] assert run["answer"] == 0.5, run run = run_code_agent("x", scripted( "\nfinal_answer(stock('durian'))\n", "\nfinal_answer(0)\n"), TOOLS) assert run["history"][0]["observation"].startswith("KeyError"), run["history"][0] # A reply with no code block at all is fed back rather than parsed as code. run = run_code_agent("x", scripted( "Thought: I think the answer is probably about six.", "\nfinal_answer(6)\n"), TOOLS) assert run["history"][0]["code"] is None, run["history"] assert "No block" in run["history"][0]["observation"], run["history"] assert run["answer"] == 6, run # Nothing ends the loop except the terminating call -- an agent that never makes it # runs to the cap and then fails, having asked the model exactly that many times. asked = [] def never_finishes(task, history): asked.append(len(history)) return "\nx = 1\n" try: run_code_agent("x", never_finishes, TOOLS, max_steps=4) except MaxStepsError: pass else: raise AssertionError("without a terminating call the run must fail at the cap") assert asked == [0, 1, 2, 3], asked # The model is given the history so it can see its own past observations. seen = [] run_code_agent("x", lambda task, history: seen.append((task, list(history))) or ( "\nprint('hi')\n" if not history else "\nfinal_answer(1)\n"), TOOLS) assert seen[0] == ("x", []), seen[0] assert seen[1][1][0]["observation"] == "hi", seen[1] # Tools are ordinary functions already in scope, not something to be looked up. run = run_code_agent("x", scripted( "\ntotals = [get_price(i) * stock(i) for i in ('apple', 'banana')]\n" "final_answer(sum(totals))\n"), TOOLS) assert run["answer"] == 6.9, run

checks.prompt: An agent using a small local model behaves badly: its code frequently raises, the errors get worse across steps rather than better, and runs end at the iteration cap with no answer. The team's first instinct is that the library is at fault. What is the most likely diagnosis and what should they check?
checks.explanation: A code-action agent is only as good as the model's coding. A weak model writes buggy snippets, and since each error is returned as an observation, the run either recovers — which is what a capable model does — or snowballs. Two mechanical things are worth checking alongside: the loop is terminated only by the special final-answer call, so a model that never emits it will always run to the cap; and the code has to arrive inside the tags the parser expects, or nothing is parsed at all. Raising the cap merely pays for more failing attempts.
options: For a code-writing agent, model coding ability dominates: a weak model produces buggy snippets, and because each failure is fed back as an observation a weak model snowballs where a capable one self-corrects — so try a capable instruction- or code-tuned model. They should also check that the model is actually calling the terminating function, since nothing else ends the loop, and that its code is wrapped in the tags the parser expects, since a differently-formatted reply will not parse at all
The compounding errors indicate the interpreter is re-executing earlier steps, which is fixed by clearing state between steps; model choice is not a significant factor
The cap is being hit because the cap is too low; raising it substantially resolves both the errors and the missing answer, since the model needs more attempts
The failures mean tools were registered without type hints, which makes the generated code call them wrongly; adding hints fixes the errors and the termination together

checks.prompt: Argue where this library is the right choice and where it is not, against three alternatives: an explicit stateful graph runtime, a role-based multi-agent framework, and this library's own structured-tool-call agent. Then advise a team building a customer-facing assistant that will take arbitrary user text and needs a tool that must never be invoked with free-form arguments, and say what they must do before shipping.
checks.expected: A correct answer must name the sweet spot and the weak spots. It wins on smallness and the code-as-action idea: a tiny, hackable, model-agnostic loop whose sweet spot is agents doing real computational work — data wrangling, arithmetic, composing several tools — where one snippet replaces several separate round trips. Against an explicit stateful graph runtime, the comparison must be that heavy orchestration is the other tool's job: branching workflows, checkpoints, durable state and human-in-the-loop pauses, with more control and more ceremony; this library is not a workflow engine. Against a role-based multi-agent framework, the comparison is opinionated personas and task orchestration out of the box versus a tight low-level loop, though simple hierarchies are possible here by handing an agent other agents as tools. Against its own structured-call agent, the point is that it is the same library with a different action representation, and it is the right choice when a capability must not be expressible as free-form code or when the backend's native structured calling is stronger. The advice must combine both halves of the scenario: the tool that must never take free-form arguments is an argument for the structured-call agent, or at least for keeping that capability out of the code interpreter; and arbitrary user text plus model-written code is the untrusted case, so before shipping they must run the code in real isolation — a container or a hosted sandbox executor — rather than the local interpreter, which is a guardrail and not a hardened sandbox. Naming a minimal import allow-list and a sensible iteration cap as further requirements is a plus.
